title: De Musica
author: Boethius

passages.original: Gaudet a euim gens modis morum similitudine. Neque enim fieri potest ut mollia duris, dura mollioribus adnectantur aut gaudeant. Sed amorem delectationemque (ut dictum est) similitudo conciliat. Unde Plato etiam maxime cavendum existimat, ne de bene morata musica aliquid permutetur. Negat enim esse ullam tantam morum in republica labem, quam paulatim de pudenti ac modesta musica invertere. Statim enim idem quoque audientium animos pati, paulatimque discedere, nullumque honesti ac recti retinere vestigium, si vel per lasciviores modos inverecundum aliquid, vel per asperiores ferox atque immane mentibus illabatur.
passages.english: For a people delights in modes through likeness of character. For it cannot happen that soft things are joined to hard, or hard to softer, or take delight in them. But, as has been said, likeness wins love and delight. Hence Plato too thinks that the greatest care must be taken that nothing be changed in well-ordered music. For he denies that there is any ruin of morals in a commonwealth so great as gradually to overturn [it] from chaste and modest music. For at once the minds of the listeners also suffer the same thing, and little by little they depart [from virtue] and keep no trace of what is honourable and right, if either something shameless glides into their minds through more wanton modes, or something fierce and savage through harsher ones.
passages.notes: "a euim" read as "enim" (stray footnote mark omitted). The clause "quam paulatim ... invertere" is elliptical; translated as "than gradually to overturn [it]".

passages.original: Nam |cum scortum in rivalis domo esset clausum, atque ille furens domum vellet amburere, cumque Pytghagoras stellarum cursus (ut ei mos nocturnus erat) inspiceret, ubi intellexit sono Phrygii modi incitatum, multis amicorum 0 admonitionibus a facinore noluisse desistere, mutari modum praecepit atque ita furentis animum adolescentis ad statum mentis pacatissimae temperavit. Quod scilicet Marcus Tullius commemorat in eo libro quem de consiliis suis composuit, aliter quidem, sed hoc modo. Sed ut aliqua similitudine adductus, maximis minima conferam, ut cum vinolenti adolescentes tibiarum etiam cantu (ut fit) instincti, mulieris pudicae fores frangerent, admonuisse tibicinam ut spondeum caneret Pythagoras dicitur;
passages.english: For when a harlot was shut up in a rival's house, and he in his frenzy wanted to burn the house down, and Pythagoras was observing the courses of the stars (as was his nightly custom), when he understood that [the youth], roused by the sound of the Phrygian mode, had refused to desist from the crime despite many warnings from his friends, he ordered the mode to be changed, and so tempered the raging youth's mind to a state of most peaceful calm. Marcus Tullius records this, in the book he composed on his own counsels, differently indeed, but in this way: "But, so that I may compare the smallest things to the greatest, led by some likeness: when drunken youths, stirred up also by the music of pipes (as happens), were breaking down the doors of a chaste woman, Pythagoras is said to have advised the piper-girl to play a spondee;
passages.notes: "Pytghagoras" read as Pythagoras; stray "0" omitted. The sentence continues into the following passage.

passages.original: Quid est enim quod illam incorpoream rationis vivacitatem corpori misceat, nisi quædam coaptatio, et veluti gravium leviumque vocum, quasi unam consonantiam efticiens, temperatio? Quid est autem aliud quod ipsius inter se partes animae conjungat, quai (ut Aristoteli placet) ex rationabili irrationabilique conjuncta est? Quid vero quod corporis elementa permisceat, aut partes sibimet rata coaptatione contineat? Sed de hac quoque posterius dicam. Tertia est musica, quae in quibusdam consistere dicitur instrumentis.
passages.english: For what is it that mixes that incorporeal liveliness of reason with the body, if not a certain fitting-together, and a tempering, as it were, of low and high sounds, producing as it were a single consonance? And what else is it that joins together the parts of the soul itself, which (as Aristotle holds) is joined from the rational and the irrational? And what is it that mingles the elements of the body, or holds its parts together with one another by a fixed fitting-together? But of this too I shall speak later. The third is the music which is said to reside in certain instruments.
How Pythagoras investigated the ratios of the consonances.

passages.original: Sed Marcus Tullius contrarium ordinem facit. Nam in vi lib. de Republica sic ait : Et natura fert ut extrema ex altera parte graviter, ex altera autem acute sonent. Quam ob causam summus ille cæli stellifer cursus, cujus conversio est concitatior acuto, et excitato movetur sono, gravissimo autem hic lunaris atque infimus. Nam terra nona, immobilis manens, ima sede semper haeret ; hic igitur Tullius terram quasi silentium ponit, scilicet immobilem. Post hanc b sui proximus a silentio est, dat Lunæ gravissimum sonum, ut sit Luna proslambanomenos. Mercurius hypate hypaton, Venus parhypate hypaton, Sol lichanos hypaton, Mars hypate meson, Jupiter parhypate meson, Saturnus lichanos meson, Coelnm ultimum mese.
passages.english: But Marcus Tullius makes the order the reverse. For in the sixth book of the Republic he says thus: "And nature brings it about that the extremes sound low at one end and high at the other. For this reason that highest star-bearing course of the heaven, whose revolution is swifter, moves with a high and excited sound, but this lunar and lowest [course] with the lowest. For the earth, the ninth, remaining motionless, always clings to the lowest seat." Here, then, Tullius places the earth as silence, that is, as motionless. After it, he gives the lowest sound to the Moon, as being nearest to silence, so that the Moon is proslambanomenos, Mercury hypate hypaton, Venus parhypate hypaton, the Sun lichanos hypaton, Mars hypate meson, Jupiter parhypate meson, Saturn lichanos meson, the outermost heaven mese.
passages.notes: "b sui" read as "quae" or similar with a stray footnote mark; sense "which is nearest to silence". The note names (proslambanomenos, hypate hypaton, etc.) are Greek terms for the strings of the Greater Perfect System, kept untranslated.

passages.english: How Plato says consonances are produced.

passages.original: Sed jam segnior, nec ita celeri, ut primo impetn emissus cucurrit, quocirca gravior quoque. Gunwgitur jam gravior rediens, nunc primum gravi sono venientisimilis occurrit, miscetur ei, unamque, g ut ait Plato, consonantiam miscet.
passages.english: But [it is] now slower, and not as swift as when it ran, sent forth with its first impulse; and therefore also lower. So when, now lower, it returns, it now for the first time meets, as like it, the low sound coming on, mixes with it, and, as Plato says, blends one consonance.
passages.notes: "impetn" read as "impetu"; "Gunwgitur" as "Cum igitur"; "venientisimilis" as "venienti similis"; stray "g" omitted.

passages.original: Omnis vero quantitas secundum Pythagoram vel continua, vel discreta est. Sed quæ continua est magnitudo appellatur, quæ discreta est multitudo. Quorum hæc est diversa et contraria pene proprietas. Multitudo enim a finita inchoans quantitate, crescens in infinita progreditur, ut nullus crescendi linis occurrat.
passages.english: Every quantity, according to Pythagoras, is either continuous or discrete. That which is continuous is called magnitude, that which is discrete multitude. The properties of these are different and almost contrary. For multitude, beginning from a finite quantity, proceeds by increasing to infinity, so that no limit to its increase is met.

passages.original: vero diatessaron ac diapente unum diapason videntur efficere, erunt quinque toni et duo spatia semitoniorum minora, quae unum tonum non videantur implere. Nonestigitur diapason consonantia constans sex tonis, ut Aristoxenus arbitratur, quod in numeris quoque dispositum evidenter apparet. Sex enim toni in ordinem disponantur, scilicet in sesquioctavis proportionibus constituti, sex vero sesquioctavce proportiones a sexto octuplo procreantur.
passages.english: [If] the diatessaron and diapente joined seem to make one diapason, there will be five tones and two minor semitone intervals, which do not seem to fill up one tone. Therefore the diapason is not a consonance consisting of six tones, as Aristoxenus thinks, which also appears clearly when set out in numbers. For let six tones be arranged in order, namely set in sesquioctave ratios; and six sesquioctave ratios are produced from the sixth octuple.
passages.notes: The opening conditional ("if ... joined") begins in the preceding context; "sesquioctavce" read as "sesquioctavae". Sesquioctave = 9:8.

passages.original: Quod si (ut ait Aristoxenus) diatessaron consonantia ex duobus tonis semitonioque conjungitur, duae diatessaron consonantiæ necessario quinque tonos efficient, et diapente ac diatessaron junctæ, sicut unum diapason jungunt, ita sex tonis continua proportione coaequantur.
passages.english: But if (as Aristoxenus says) the consonance diatessaron is composed of two tones and a semitone, two diatessaron consonances will necessarily make five tones, and the diapente and diatessaron joined, just as they make up one diapason, so are made equal to six tones in continuous proportion.

passages.original: Quomodo Aristoxenus vel tonum dividat, vel genera f ejusque divisionis dispositio.
passages.english: How Aristoxenus divides the tone, or the genera, and the arrangement of his division.
passages.notes: The stray 'f' after 'genera' appears to be a footnote mark or scanning error and has been omitted. The syntax of the heading is loose ('vel genera ... ejusque divisionis dispositio'); it is rendered as a list of topics.

passages.original: Semitonium, Toni medietas Semitonium. Omnium intervallorum quae in tono sunt secundum Aristoxenum divisio.
passages.english: Semitone: the half of a tone [is] a semitone. The division, according to Aristoxenus, of all the intervals that are in a tone.
passages.notes: This appears to be a chapter heading combined with a diagram label ('Semitonium, Toni medietas Semitonium'); the wording is fragmentary.

passages.original: Sunt igitur secundumhuncordinem differentiæ permixtorum generum sex. Una quidem enharmonii, 3 autem chromatici, id est chromatici mollis, et chromaticihemioln, et chromatici thonisei. Duae vero reliquæ diatonici, mollis atque incitati. Quorum omnium talis secundum Aristoxenum divisio est. Quoniam enim quarta pars toni diesis enharmonios nuncupari prædicta est, quoniamque Aristoxenus nou voces ipsas inter se comparat, sed differentiam vocum intervallumque metitur, et secundum eum tonus est duodecim unitatum, hujus igitur erit pars quarta diesis enharmonios tres.
passages.english: According to this order, then, there are six differences among the mixed genera: one of the enharmonic; three of the chromatic, namely the soft chromatic, the hemiolic chromatic and the tonic chromatic; and the remaining two of the diatonic, the soft and the sharp. The division of all of these according to Aristoxenus is as follows. Since the quarter of a tone was said earlier to be called the enharmonic diesis, and since Aristoxenus does not compare the notes themselves with each other but measures the difference and interval between the notes, and according to him the tone is twelve units, the quarter of this, the enharmonic diesis, will be three.

passages.original: Quemadmodum Ptolemæus et Aristoxeni et Architæ tetrachordorum divisiones deprehendat.
passages.english: How Ptolemy finds fault with the divisions of the tetrachords both of Aristoxenus and of Archytas.
passages.notes: 'Architæ' is taken as Archytas. 'Deprehendat' could also mean 'detects' or 'exposes'; in context it refers to Ptolemy's criticism of their divisions.

passages.original: Aristoxenum vero culpat, quoniam in chromate molli et in chromate hemiolio tales posuerit primas secundasque a gravi nervo proportiones, quae a se a minimo et quantum sensus non possit internoscere distarent. Est quippe proportio prima in chromatis mollis, f prima divisione secundum Aristoxenum octo, at in chromate hemiolio novem. Sed octo ad novem unitatis diiferentia distant. Est autem tonus totus 24 unitatibus secundum positionem vel propositionem quorum unitas 2r est. Primae igitur a gravi inter se proportiones chromatis mollis, et chromatis hemiolii 24 parte toni distant, quod propter brevitatem differentiæ nullo modo sentit auditus.
passages.english: But he blames Aristoxenus because in the soft chromatic and in the hemiolic chromatic he set first and second proportions, [counting] from the lowest string, of such a kind that they would differ from each other by the least amount, and by an amount which the sense could not distinguish. For the first proportion in the soft chromatic, in the first division according to Aristoxenus, is eight, but in the hemiolic chromatic nine. But eight and nine differ by a difference of one unit. Now the whole tone consists of 24 units according to the setting-out or proposition, of which the unit is 1/24. Therefore the first proportions from the low [string] of the soft chromatic and of the hemiolic chromatic differ from each other by a 24th part of a tone, which, because of the smallness of the difference, the hearing in no way perceives.
passages.notes: The stray 'f' before 'prima divisione' is taken as a footnote mark and omitted. 'quorum unitas 2r est' is evidently a scanning error, probably for a fraction such as 1/24 (the unit being a 24th part of the tone); translated accordingly. 'secundum positionem vel propositionem' is ambiguous (the arrangement or proposition of the numbers in the diagram). 'a se a minimo' is read as 'a se minimo', 'by the least amount'. 'diiferentia' read as 'differentia'.
